newsitem.title: USA: Senators unveil kids health insurance bill.
newsitem.headline: Senators unveil kids health insurance bill.

text.p: Two leading senators on Thursday launched a bipartisan effort to extend health care to at least half the nation's 10 million uninsured children, raising the odds Congress will act on the issue this session.

Massachusetts Democrat Edward Kennedy and Utah Republican Orrin Hatch unveiled legislation to provide $20 billion in grants to states over five years for public-private efforts to cover uninsured children.

The measure would be funded through a 43-cents-per-pack increase in the federal cigarette tax, as well as higher levies on other tobacco products. An additional $10 billion generated by the tax would be used for deficit reduction.

"Uninsured children don't get timely care, and many receive no care at all. Too often the result is needless suffering, stunted growth and a lifetime of disability or early death," Kennedy told a news conference.
While a spate of legislation has been introduced on the issue, the Kennedy-Hatch bill is the first major bipartisan effort to address childrens' health care.
President Clinton's balanced budget plan includes an initiative to extend care to as many as 5 million children, mainly by expanding Medicaid programme for the poor.
Hatch said that as a Republican he was normally loathe to advocate higher taxes. But he called it past time for Congress to address the issue of care for kids.
"Some people will ask why I'm doing this and with Ted Kennedy no less. The answer is it's the right thing to do," Hatch said. "Lack of health care for our children is a nightmare for parents."
The legislation came as the Census Bureau released new data showing nearly 10 million children, or close to 14 percent of Americans younger than 18, lacked health insurance.
Most uninsured children live in working families that have too much money to qualify for the Medicaid health programme for the poor, but too little to purchase private health care.

Hatch and Kennedy said they had both had to bend to reach consensus, with the conservative Hatch insisting the bill include deficit reduction. They agreed to resist efforts from the left to expand the bill and from the right to limit it.
The grant programme would be voluntary. States that participated would have to put up 10 to 20 percent of the funding.
Instead of a government-run programme, states would contract with private insurers to offer coverage.
Kennedy and Hatch said the bill would provide direct aid to 5 million children. The total who would receive insurance could be millions higher, depending on what states did.
The federal cigarette tax is 24 cents a pack. Lawmakers have tried in the past to raise tobacco taxes to pay for health care, with limited success.
"Having a Hatch-Kennedy bill increases the odds of something happening ... what's not going to happen is that tax increase," said a top Republican aide.

Pennsylvania Republican Sen. Arlen Specter introduced a separate bill Thursday to expand care to 4 million children in working poor families. His bill calls for $10 billion over five years for states to provide vouchers to buy insurance.
